passage: I typed my email password into the page, pressed enter, and knew straight away. The page had loaded slowly and the address at the top looked odd. My stomach dropped, and for a few seconds I just stared. Then I stopped panicking and started doing things. First I changed the password on the real site. Then I signed out of every other device. I switched on two-step verification. Finally I went to find Papa, Jatin to everyone else, and said, “I made a mistake, and I think I've fixed most of it, but the bank should know.” He rang the bank that evening while I sat beside him. I still felt silly, but I'd rather say it early than late. — Deepak

passage:
Computer teacher's note, Thursday, after period six
During the free period Wasim came to my desk white-faced. He had entered his login for the school learning portal on a page that came from a message, then noticed the web address was wrong. What struck me is what he had already done before reaching me. In the eight minutes since, he had changed the password on the real site, used the “log out of all devices” button, and switched on two-step verification with his phone. He showed me each screen.
He also asked whether the same password was used anywhere else. It was: his email. We changed that together. Then he phoned his father from my desk, because that email receives the family's bank alerts, and his father called the bank on the number from his card while we waited.
Afterwards Vinita, at the next computer, asked him how to switch on two-step verification.

qa.q: How many minutes passed between the slip and reaching the teacher's desk?
What does Wasim's white face suggest when he reached the desk?
qa.a: It suggests he was frightened and shaken, even though he had already acted quickly and sensibly.

qa.q: What could Wasim do next to lower the risk further?
qa.a: Use a different password for each account, so one slip cannot open the email or anything else.

qa.q: How might Vinita see what happened at the next computer?
qa.a: Vinita sees a quick, calm clean-up and wants the same protection, asking how to switch on two-step verification.

grounding: A teacher notes a student who entered a login on a fake page changing the password, logging out other devices, adding two-step verification and telling a parent to warn the bank.

passage:
Sunday
Close call today, and I think I handled it.
Around four, a message said my email storage was full and I should log in to keep my files. I logged in on the page. Only after pressing enter did I see the address had an extra letter in it. My hands went cold.
What I did, in order: opened the real site myself and changed the password. Hit “sign out everywhere”. Damini showed me where to turn on two-step verification, so now a code comes to my phone. Then I went to Mummy even though I wanted to hide in my room, because my email gets the bank's messages about the family account. She called the bank from the number on her card, and they're watching the account.
Total time: maybe twenty minutes. Nothing strange since. Still shaky.
– Manoj

qa.q: What did the message say about the email?
qa.a: That the email storage was full and Manoj should log in to keep the files.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel on noticing the extra letter, and later that day?
qa.a: Manoj's hands went cold with fear, and hours later Manoj still felt shaky, though relieved at having handled it.

qa.q: What else could Manoj do in the coming days?
qa.a: Check the email's recent sign-in list and change any other account that used the same password.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Manoj coming to her?
qa.a: Mummy is probably relieved to hear within minutes, since that let her warn the bank before anything went wrong.

grounding: Shows a student who entered a login on a fake page changing the password at once, signing out other devices, turning on two-step verification and telling a parent.
